content.title: Clinical Guidelines as a Continuous Work in Progress: Moving at the Speed of Science
content.text: The American College of Cardiology (ACC) and the American Heart Association (AHA) employ a rigorous methodology for development of clinical practice guidelines.1 The goal of this joint effort is to produce the highest quality guidelines that are clinically relevant, timely, trustworthy in scientific rigor, transparent in the development process, and accessible for clinicians in daily practice. Such a robust methodology requires sufficient time for a comprehensive literature search, expert consensus building following review of the latest science, development of evidence-based recommendations, peer review, society policy approvals, and ultimately, the publication process itself. Thus, it is not surprising that scientific discovery may at times outpace the guideline development to publication timeline. This was certainly the case with publication of the results of the VESALIUS-CV (Effect of Evolocumab in Patients at High Cardiovascular Risk Without Prior Myocardial Infarction or Stroke) trial2 relative to the publication timeline of the 2026 ACC/AHA/ Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia.3VESALIUS-CV is a large (N=12,257), rigorously conducted, international, randomized, placebo-controlled trial conducted in patients at high cardiovascular risk but without prior myocardial infarction (MI) or stroke. The findings have important implications for the prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) events. Patients with coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, or at least moderate atherosclerosis by coronary artery calcium score (CAC) without prior MI or stroke, as well as patients with high-risk diabetes (chronic insulin therapy, duration ≥10 years, or microvascular disease) and at least one additional high-risk feature, were randomized to more intensive lowering of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) with evolocumab versus placebo added to baseline statin therapy with or without ezetimibe.4Lipid criteria for enrollment included LDL-C ≥90 mg/dL, non–high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ≥120 mg/dL, or apolipoprotein B ≥80 mg/dL, presumably on maximally tolerated statin therapy. The dual primary endpoints were a composite of MI, ischemic stroke, or death from coronary heart disease (3-point major adverse cardiovascular events [MACE]) and a composite of 3-point MACE or ischemia-driven arterial revascularization (4-point MACE). The median baseline LDL-C in the overall population was 122 mg/dL. The addition of evolocumab resulted in a 55% mean LDL-C reduction (63 mg/dL) with a median achieved LDL-C of 45 mg/dL, while the median achieved LDL-C in the placebo group was 109 mg/dL. Median follow up was 4.6 years. Highly significant reductions in both 3-point MACE (HR: 0.75; 95% CI: 0.65-0.86; P < 0.001) and 4-point MACE (HR: 0.81; 95% CI: 0.73 to 0.89; P < 0.001) were observed in the evolocumab group. The absolute risk reductions were 1.8% for 3-point MACE (number needed to treat = 56), and 2.8% for the 4-point MACE (number needed to treat = 36) over 4.6 years. There were no between-group differences in safety events.The results of the VESALIUS-CV trial provide important insights into a broader spectrum of patients earlier in the atherosclerotic disease process than previously studied and expand our understanding of at-risk individuals who benefit from more intensive lipid lowering therapy. Overall, 67% of participants had qualifying atherosclerosis without prior MI or stroke. In addition, VESALIUS-CV included a large population with significant cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome risk. Forty nine percent of participants had high-risk diabetes, and 33% (n=4001) had high-risk diabetes without known qualifying atherosclerosis. Of the two-thirds of participants with qualifying atherosclerosis, 1000 individuals had CAC ≥100 Agatston units (AU), of whom 544 people had CAC ≥300 AU. There were no between-group differences in outcomes based on qualifying disease, baseline lipid lowering therapy, or baseline LDL-C.The practice-changing findings of VESALIUS-CV have important implications for the 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia, as the results were not yet available at the time of final guideline review and approval.3 The current guideline differentiates between individuals with ASCVD at very high risk and ASCVD not at very high risk based on the combined inclusion criteria for FOURIER (Further Cardiovascular Outcomes Research With PCSK9 Inhibition in Subjects With Elevated Risk) and ODYSSEY OUTCOMES (Evaluation of Cardiovascular Outcomes After an Acute Coronary Syndrome During Treatment With Alirocumab).5,6 However, the 2026 guideline authors note that the majority of patients in clinical practice who have ASCVD are at very high risk, with prior MACE and additional high-risk features (recommended LDL-C goal of <55 mg/dL). Only a small percentage of patients with ASCVD are not at very high risk (recommended LDL-C goal <70 mg/dL).The significant cardiovascular benefits with more intensive lowering of LDL-C to <55 mg/dL in patients without previous MI or stroke in VESALIUS-CV now blur the distinction between ASCVD risk categories when defining a “goal” LDL-C value. Thus, future updates to the 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Dyslipidemia Guideline should include a single pathway of care for all patients with ASCVD (including prior MACE as well as coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, or at least moderate atherosclerosis on imaging without prior MI or stroke) with an optimal LDL-C goal of <55 mg/dL to be achieved via pharmacotherapy as well as lifestyle optimization.VESALIUS-CV also redefines the benefits of more intensive LDL-C–lowering therapy to an LDL-C goal of <55 mg/dL in patients with high-risk diabetes and ≥1 additional high-risk feature. Future guideline revisions should include an evidence-based recommendation for more intensive LDL-C lowering in this high-risk population.The 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Dyslipidemia Guideline includes recommendations for management of patients with moderate subclinical atherosclerosis with a goal LDL-C <70 mg/dL for those with a CAC score ≥100 AU and an optional goal of LDL-C <55 mg/dL for those with CAC score ≥300 AU. The levels of evidence for these recommendations are strengthened by the results of VESALIUS-CV.As Chair and Vice Chair of the 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline, we are grateful for this opportunity to clarify the publication timeline and the implications of the rapidly evolving scientific base that supports our current recommendations and informs future updates. The new modular format of the guidelines is intended to make it simpler and more efficient to update guidelines on an annual basis to remain relevant, timely, and trustworthy. Appropriate revisions to this guideline are planned. This is a perfect example of the strength of the ACC/AHA guideline methodology to keep the guidelines continuously moving at the speed of science!Funding Support and Author DisclosuresThe authors have reported that they have no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.References1.Otto C.M., Abdullah A.R., Davis L.L., et al. 2025 ACC/AHA clinical practice guidelines core principles and development process: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines.
